claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength.
The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi are governed by extensive dynamic recovery.
The relevant starting material is a single-phase solid solution with uniform elemental distribution.
The homogeneous solid solution lacks strong secondary-particle pinning.
The homogeneous solid-solution structure impedes forest-dislocation interactions.
The absence of strong dislocation obstacles enables high dislocation mobility.
Dynamic recovery proceeds through dislocation annihilation and cross-slip.
Rapid dynamic recovery prevents substantial accumulation of forest dislocations.
Limited forest-dislocation accumulation reduces work hardening, hardness, and strength.
Dynamic recovery allows favorable plasticity despite low hardness and strength.
Lower strain rates increase dynamic recovery.
Higher test temperatures increase dynamic recovery.
More pronounced dynamic recovery produces lower apparent work hardening and hardness.
Higher strain rates or lower temperatures temporarily suppress dynamic recovery.
Suppression of dynamic recovery at higher strain rates or lower temperatures causes a modest increase in strength.
CoCrFeNiTi remains substantially softer than materials containing stronger obstacles to dislocation motion.
At room temperature and moderate strain rate, equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has high plasticity and limited work hardening.
Possible nanoscale heterogeneities or deformation-induced phase transformations may also influence hardness and strength.

contradictions.description: The prediction allows increased strength when high strain rate or low temperature suppresses recovery, whereas the falsification rule treats an increase in work hardening under those same conditions as potentially falsifying. The distinction between the predicted modest response and a falsifying response is not quantitatively defined.

The hypothesis is restricted to conditions without phase transformation or precipitation, but the appearance of secondary phases is listed as a falsifier. Such an observation would instead place the test outside the stated applicability boundary unless phase formation occurred under conditions explicitly asserted to remain within it.
